raw_segments.text: The book of Job hath no mark in it of the time wherein it was written, and though it
appear sufficiently, Exekiel 14.14 and James 5.11, that he was no fain person, yet the
book itself seemeth not to be a history, but a treatise concerning a question in ancient
time much disputed.
Why wicked men have often prospered in this world, and good men have been afflicted?
And it is the most probably because from the beginning to the third verse of the third
beginneth, the Hebrew is, as St. Jerome testifies, in prose, and from thence to the sixth verse
of the last chapter in Hexameter, Verses, and the rest of that chapter again in prose,
so that the dispute is all in verse, and the prose is added but as a preface in the beginning
and an epilogue in the end.

such as come to comfort them as his friends, but in philosophy, especially moral philosophy,
in ancient time frequent.
